content_html:
Status: first release, November 2026. Every section was researched against primary sources and reviewed by the author, and CI checks every change: links, structure, diagrams, and that every lab runs. The few claims that couldn't be confirmed against a primary source are listed, with the sections that use them, in PLAN.md. Reviews and corrections are welcome; please include a source.

Learn how to design systems built on large language models: the trade-offs, the components, and the patterns that have converged across the industry, along with the ones that are still moving.

Motivation

Learn how to design AI systems that hold up in production. Prepare for the AI system design conversation.

Building on models is now a core engineering skill, and the field moves fast. Most of what's written about it is a product announcement, a framework tutorial or a single team's experience. This primer is an organised collection of what has converged across providers and researchers, with every trade-off named and every number dated and sourced.

It is modelled on Donne Martin's System Design Primer: the same arc of method, trade-offs, components, solved designs and reference numbers, rebuilt for systems whose core component is probabilistic, priced per token, and open to prompt injection.

Learn how to design AI systems. Each topic is a short page you can read in ten minutes, with a diagram, when to use it, when not to, and its disadvantages. A deep dive per topic holds the provider survey, numbers, risk controls and cloud mappings.

Prepare for the AI system design conversation, in an interview or a design review. Work through the method, the solved designs and the practice questions.

Anki flashcards

Every page ends in question-and-answer flashcards. Build the deck with either command (standard library only):

python3 scripts/primer.py anki         # writes build/ai-system-design-primer.apkg: double-click to import
python3 scripts/primer.py flashcards   # writes build/flashcards.tsv: plain text for Anki's File > Import

The package has one sub-deck per part. Re-importing a newer build updates answers in place and keeps your review history; a reworded question arrives as a new card. Cards are tagged by section and maturity, so you can study one part, or suspend maturity::frontier cards when they go stale.

Contributing

Learn from the community.

Pull requests are welcome to fix errors, improve sections and add new ones. Read STYLE.md for how sections are researched and written (learner-first, several providers per topic, every claim sourced) and CONTRIBUTING.md for the mechanics. Decisions about the primer itself are recorded in adr/. Work still to do is in ROADMAP.md.

How to approach an AI system design question

How to tackle an AI system design question, in an interview or a design review.

The classic four steps, with two changes: the quality bar comes first, because a model-backed feature is right only some of the time; and hardening is its own step, because prompt injection, data leakage and runaway agents are design constraints, not add-ons.

  1. Use cases, constraints and the quality bar. Who, what, how many, how fast, what data, and how you'll know it works.
  2. Back-of-the-envelope. Tokens per request, requests per second, cost per day, latency.
  3. High-level design on the complexity ladder. Single call → workflow → single agent → multi-agent. Start at the lowest rung that meets the bar.
  4. Core components. Retrieval, context, tools, model choice, output checks.
  5. Harden. Which legs of the lethal trifecta are present, and which does the design break?
  6. Scale and optimise. Bottlenecks in order; caching, routing, batching.

Appendix

  • Numbers every AI engineer should know: tokens, speed, cost ratios, memory, retrieval and eval figures, each dated and sourced.
  • Cloud mapping: each capability on Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, OpenAI, Anthropic and open source.
  • Pattern crosswalk: the same patterns under each provider's and author's names.
  • Governance crosswalk: OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10, FINOS, EU AI Act, mapped to primer sections.
  • Real-world architectures: engineering write-ups and independent studies.
  • Glossary and changelog.

How this primer differs from the original, and from a blog post

  • Trade-offs first. Every pattern says which trade-off it moves and in which direction.
  • Quality bar first. Evals are part of the method, not an afterthought.
  • Maturity is labelled and dated. Each page carries last_verified and review_by; the checker fails when a review is overdue. Frontier pages are reviewed every three months.
  • Several providers on every topic. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, AWS and Microsoft, with the names each uses.
  • Vendor-neutral prose. Product names live in the deep dives and the cloud mapping.
  • Risk and controls on every topic, with the evidence an auditor would ask for.
  • Runnable labs with predictions recorded before the run.

Contact info

Open an issue to discuss errors, missing topics or new solved designs. Report security problems, or guidance that would make a system less safe, privately as described in SECURITY.md. Participation is covered by the Code of Conduct.

  • All diagrams and charts are original to this repository and covered by the content licence.
  • Code (scripts/, the lab scripts and the CI workflow) is licensed under the MIT License.
  • Contributions are accepted under the same terms. The reasoning is in ADR 0008.

How this was written

The author researched and wrote this primer with an AI assistant, and reviewed every section. The method is in STYLE.md: primary sources from several providers for every claim, a dated last_verified on every page, runnable labs instead of asserted numbers, and a public list of what isn't yet verified. Mistakes are still possible; please report them with a source.

content_html_zh:
Status: first release, November 2026. Every section was researched against primary sources and reviewed by the author, and CI checks every change: links, structure, diagrams, and that every lab runs. The few claims that couldn't be confirmed against a primary source are listed, with the sections that use them, in PLAN.md. Reviews and corrections are welcome; please include a source.

Learn how to design systems built on large language models: the trade-offs, the components, and the patterns that have converged across the industry, along with the ones that are still moving.

动机

Learn how to design AI systems that hold up in production. Prepare for the AI system design conversation.

Building on models is now a core engineering skill, and the field moves fast. Most of what's written about it is a product announcement, a framework tutorial or a single team's experience. This primer is an organised collection of what has converged across providers and researchers, with every trade-off named and every number dated and sourced.

It is modelled on Donne Martin's System Design Primer: the same arc of method, trade-offs, components, solved designs and reference numbers, rebuilt for systems whose core component is probabilistic, priced per token, and open to prompt injection.

Learn how to design AI systems. Each topic is a short page you can read in ten minutes, with a diagram, when to use it, when not to, and its disadvantages. A deep dive per topic holds the provider survey, numbers, risk controls and cloud mappings.

Prepare for the AI system design conversation, in an interview or a design review. Work through the method, the solved designs and the practice questions.

Anki flashcards

Every page ends in question-and-answer flashcards. Build the deck with either command (standard library only):

python3 scripts/primer.py anki         # writes build/ai-system-design-primer.apkg: double-click to import
python3 scripts/primer.py flashcards   # writes build/flashcards.tsv: plain text for Anki's File > Import

The package has one sub-deck per part. Re-importing a newer build updates answers in place and keeps your review history; a reworded question arrives as a new card. Cards are tagged by section and maturity, so you can study one part, or suspend maturity::frontier cards when they go stale.

How to approach an AI system design question

How to tackle an AI system design question, in an interview or a design review.

The classic four steps, with two changes: the quality bar comes first, because a model-backed feature is right only some of the time; and hardening is its own step, because prompt injection, data leakage and runaway agents are design constraints, not add-ons.

  1. Use cases, constraints and the quality bar. Who, what, how many, how fast, what data, and how you'll know it works.
  2. Back-of-the-envelope. Tokens per request, requests per second, cost per day, latency.
  3. High-level design on the complexity ladder. Single call → workflow → single agent → multi-agent. Start at the lowest rung that meets the bar.
  4. Core components. Retrieval, context, tools, model choice, output checks.
  5. Harden. Which legs of the lethal trifecta are present, and which does the design break?
  6. Scale and optimise. Bottlenecks in order; caching, routing, batching.
